summary: Defines the syntax of Uniform Resource Names, persistent location-independent identifiers under the urn URI scheme. It specifies how to decide if two URNs are equivalent, how to define a URN namespace, and how namespace identifiers are registered with IANA. It replaces RFC 2141 and RFC 3406.

eli5.summary: A URN is like a person's name rather than their home address. It stays the same even when they move, so you can always find them.

questions: how to register a urn namespace
subtitle: The syntax, comparison rules and namespace registration process for names that are meant to outlast their locations.

tldr.problem: Persistent, location-independent names need one agreed syntax and a managed way to create namespaces, and the older URN specifications predated the modern URI syntax.
tldr.mechanism: URNs have the form urn:NID:NSS, with optional r-, q- and f-components. They are compared by a defined equivalence procedure, and new namespaces are registered with IANA using a template and Expert Review.
tldr.outcome: RFC 8141 obsoletes RFC 2141 and RFC 3406. Every URN and namespace valid under the older documents remains valid.

facts.label: Informal NID form
facts.value: urn- followed by a number, e.g. urn-7

today: RFC 8141 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 2141 and RFC 3406, and no later RFC is listed as replacing or updating it.

sections.title: What a URN Is
sections.content:
A Uniform Resource Name (URN) is a URI under the urn scheme and a particular URN namespace. The intent is that it will be a persistent, location-independent resource identifier. A URN namespace is a collection of names, each of which is unique, assigned in a consistent and managed way, and assigned according to a common definition. Some namespaces create names that exist only as URNs, while others wrap names from other systems such as ISBNs, ISSNs or RFCs.

The document rests on two assumptions: assigning a URN is a managed process, and the space of namespaces is itself managed. Starting a string with urn: is not enough. The namespace identifier must be registered under these rules, and the rest of the name must follow that namespace's rules.

RFC 8141 combines URN syntax and namespace registration in one place. It replaces RFC 2141 (syntax) and RFC 3406 (namespace definition). Where its reading of URNs seems to conflict with RFC 3986, URNs should be interpreted by this document.
sections.eli5: A URN is a name that never changes, like a book's title, instead of an address that changes whenever the book moves to a new shelf.

sections.title: URN Syntax
sections.content:
A URN has an assigned-name: urn, a colon, the namespace identifier (NID), a colon, and the namespace specific string (NSS). An example is urn:example:foo. The NID is unique across the whole urn scheme and is case insensitive, and the NSS is unique within its namespace. Together they make the URN globally unique.

The syntax follows URI rules but does not allow characters outside the ASCII range directly. They must be percent-encoded, and URNs passed between systems MUST use UTF-8 further encoded as RFC 3986 requires. The NSS can now contain /, so a hierarchical name like 1/406/47452/2 can be carried as urn:example:1/406/47452/2.

Colons in the NSS have no built-in meaning. In urn:example:apple:pear:plum:cherry the NSS is the whole string apple:pear:plum:cherry, and any structure is up to the namespace. Software that does not know a namespace's encoding rules MUST NOT build URNs from names in another identifier system.
sections.eli5: A URN has three parts like a mailing label: the word "urn", which club the name belongs to, and the name inside that club.

sections.title: The r-, q- and f-Components
sections.content:
Three optional components can follow the assigned-name. Clients are meant to treat them the same way for every URN, and none of them counts when comparing URNs.

  • The r-component, introduced by ?+, passes parameters to URN resolution services. RFC 8141 only defines its syntax and reserves it for future use, and it SHOULD NOT be used before its semantics are standardized.
  • The q-component, introduced by ?=, passes parameters to the named resource or the system serving it. A resolver that returns a locator URI copies the q-component into that URI's query. Resolution systems MUST NOT require q-component information.
  • The f-component, introduced by the number sign (#) names a location or region inside the resource and has the same syntax as a URI fragment. Clients SHOULD NOT pass it to resolution services unless those services also retrieve and interpret objects.

If a component is undefined or meaningless for a given namespace or resource, the behavior of that URN is not defined.
sections.eli5: After the name you can add notes: one for the helper who finds the thing, one for the thing itself, and one that points at a page or chapter inside it.

sections.title: Deciding When Two URNs Are Equivalent
sections.content:
Two URNs are URN-equivalent if their assigned-name portions are octet-by-octet equal after case normalization of three things: the scheme urn (lower case), the NID (lower case), and any percent-encoded characters in the NSS (upper case for the hex digits A-F). Percent-encoded characters MUST NOT be decoded for the comparison. Any r-, q- or f-component MUST be ignored.

A namespace definition MAY add further equivalence rules, such as treating the NSS as case insensitive. Such rules can only remove false negatives and MUST NOT make two URNs that this procedure treats as equivalent come out as different.

The RFC's examples show the effect: urn:example:a123,z456, URN:example:a123,z456 and urn:EXAMPLE:a123,z456 match. A different NSS case or a different percent-encoding does not, and neither does a look-alike character such as U+0430 CYRILLIC SMALL LETTER A in place of a Latin a.
sections.eli5: Two names count as the same if they only differ in capital letters in the club part. But if the actual name inside changes at all, even one letter, they are different.

sections.title: Formal and Informal Namespaces
sections.content:
A namespace comes in two types. In a formal namespace the registrant chooses the NID, which MUST NOT already be registered, MUST NOT start with urn- or X-, and MUST be more than two characters long without starting with two letters and a hyphen. Organizations assigning formal URNs SHOULD show stability, competency and a commitment never to reassign existing URNs.

In an informal namespace IANA assigns the NID as urn- followed by a number, for example urn-7. The number is ASCII digits, has no leading zeros and must keep the NID within the length limit.

Within a namespace, a name is never assigned to more than one resource and never reassigned, even if the name is deprecated. A single resource can still have more than one URN, in the same or in different namespaces.
sections.eli5: Some clubs get to pick their own club name. Others get a number handed out by the registrar, like "club 7".

sections.title: Registering a Namespace
sections.content:
The registration policy for formal namespaces is Expert Review. The registrant fills out the template in Appendix A (purpose, syntax, assignment, security and privacy, interoperability, resolution, documentation and optional additional information) and sends it to the urn@ietf.org discussion list. If the Designated Experts approve and no standardization is involved, IANA registers the NID. Registrants SHOULD also provide a stable specification.

A fast track exists for recognized standards development organizations, scientific societies and similar bodies. Reviews on the list are strictly advisory, the body decides when the application is mature, and then asks IANA to register it. The IESG decides whether to recognize such a body.

RFC 8141 also updates the registration of the urn URI scheme as permanent, with the IETF as change controller, and replaces the old discussion list from RFC 3406 with urn@ietf.org.
sections.eli5: To start a new naming club you fill in a form, let experts comment, and then the registrar adds it to the official list.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
A namespace definition has to account for security and privacy issues in assigning, using and resolving its names. One example is that some resolvers might give special meaning to certain NSS characters. The template section on this lists the consequences of false positives and false negatives in equivalence comparison, leakage of private information when names cross the public Internet, and directory harvesting.

Most URN namespaces declare public information with a relatively low security profile, but there is always a danger of spoofing and misinformation. The RFC says information in these declarations ought to be taken as advisory.
sections.eli5: A name list is public, so someone could write a fake entry. Treat what it says as a hint and double check.

sections.title: Changes from RFC 2141 and RFC 3406
sections.content:
Compared with RFC 2141, the syntax is aligned with RFC 3986, allows /, ? and (#) that were reserved for future use, adds the r-component for resolution services, disallows a hyphen at the end of the NID, and allows /, ~ and & in the NSS. It also formally registers urn as a URI scheme.

Compared with RFC 3406, the policy for formal namespaces is relaxed from IETF Review to Expert Review, the experimental X- category is removed, and the registration template is simplified. All URN namespaces and URNs valid under the earlier specifications remain valid.
sections.eli5: This is the updated rulebook. It lets names use a few more characters and makes it easier to start a new naming club.

viz.caption: BASIC URN SYNTAX IN ABNF (RFC 8141, SECTION 2)

data.title: URN ABNF
data.code:
namestring    = assigned-name
                [ rq-components ]
                [ "#" f-component ]
assigned-name = "urn" ":" NID ":" NSS
NID           = (alphanum) 0*30(ldh) (alphanum)
ldh           = alphanum / "-"
NSS           = pchar *(pchar / "/")
rq-components = [ "?+" r-component ]
                [ "?=" q-component ]
r-component   = pchar *( pchar / "/" / "?" )
q-component   = pchar *( pchar / "/" / "?" )
f-component   = fragment
